passage: I'm Sabina, and this is what I saw in the canteen on Tuesday. A group at the next table started mocking Dorjee, a first-year, about where he comes from, doing a sing-song imitation of his speech. Dorjee went very still. Karthik was sitting two seats from them with his fork in the air. He said nothing. His jaw was tight and he stared at his plate, and he left half his lunch. I can't say exactly what he was feeling. Twenty minutes later I saw Karthik find Dorjee outside the library. I couldn't hear all of it, but I caught, "That wasn't right, and I should have said something." On Thursday, when the same table started up again, Karthik said, "Stop that," before anyone else did.

qa.q: Who was sitting two seats from the group that mocked Dorjee?
qa.a: Karthik was sitting two seats from them.

qa.q: What might Karthik have been feeling while he stared at his plate?
qa.a: Possibly uneasy and guilty, since his jaw was tight, he left half his lunch and later apologised, though Sabina says she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did Karthik do afterwards that helped?
qa.a: He checked on Dorjee outside the library and, on Thursday, spoke up against the mockery himself.

qa.q: How might Dorjee have felt when Karthik came to talk?
qa.a: Possibly relieved to be noticed after going very still, since someone acknowledged that the mockery was wrong.

grounding: A bystander who watched a boy insulted for his background stays silent, feels guilty, then checks on him and backs him up next time.

passage:
Dear Chinmay,

I've been trying to write this for three days. On Friday, in the lab, when Suresh sir's assistant mocked your eyes and asked if you ate dogs in Manipur, I was right there. I heard it. And I looked at my screen and said nothing.

Afterwards I told myself it wasn't my business, that you'd handle it. But I saw your face when you left. I've felt sick about it since.

Zainab asked me yesterday why I was so quiet, and when I told her, she said, "Then go and tell him." So I'm telling you: I'm sorry. What he said was racist and wrong, and my silence helped it.

I've written down what I heard, with the time. If you decide to complain to the department, I'll be your witness. And next time, I won't look at my screen.

Samir

qa.q: Where was Samir when the insult happened?
qa.a: Samir was right there in the lab.

qa.q: How has Samir felt since staying silent?
qa.a: Samir has felt sick with guilt, especially after seeing Chinmay's face when he left.

qa.q: What steps is Samir taking to make up for the silence?
qa.a: Samir apologises, names the insult as racist, has written down what was heard, and offers to be a witness if Chinmay complains.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when nobody in the lab spoke up?
qa.a: Chinmay may have felt humiliated and alone, as if no one in the room thought the insult mattered.

grounding: The letter shows a young person who stayed silent while someone was insulted for his background, checking on him, offering to back a report and promising to speak up next time.

passage:
This happened last month and I still think about it, so let me tell you properly. It's Kamal. I was on the night train to Patna with my hostel-mate Saurabh. A group of men in the next berth started on him because of his village accent. "Gaon ka gawaar," one said. "These people make the trains dirty." They laughed. Saurabh went red and stared out the window.

And I pretended to sleep. I lay there with my eyes shut and told myself it was none of my business.

In the morning I couldn't look at him. At the station I finally said, "I'm sorry. I heard all of it. I should have said something." He shrugged, but his voice was tight. "Everyone always pretends to sleep."

That stuck. Since then, twice, I've said "That's enough" to someone on a bus. It's scary. It's better than pretending to sleep.

qa.a: The night train was going to Patna.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel the next morning?
qa.a: Kamal felt ashamed and guilty, unable to look at Saurabh after pretending to sleep.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who has stayed silent like Kamal?
qa.a: Check on the person, apologise honestly, and back them up next time, as Kamal later did by saying "That's enough" on buses.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see bystanders who stay quiet?
qa.a: Saurabh sees them as common and disappointing, saying everyone always pretends to sleep, which shows how alone he felt.

grounding: The monologue shows a young person who watched someone insulted for his background and said nothing, then checks on him and speaks up next time.
